topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Finding a missing number in addition
topic.description: Understand subtraction as finding an unknown addend (e.g. 10 − 8 = ? is the same as 8 + ? = 10)
evidence: Solve 10 − 8 by thinking 'what do I add to 8 to make 10?'
Explain that subtraction can be thought of as a missing-addend problem
Use known addition facts to solve related subtraction problems
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} see that '10 − 8 = ?' is the same as asking 'what do I add to 8 to reach 10?' — so they can use their adding knowledge to help with subtraction?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Subtraction as an unknown-addend problem — understanding that 10 − 8 = ? is the same question as 8 + ? = 10, so subtraction can be solved by finding the missing part / counting on. Ages 6–7, a key bridge from take-away to the additive structure.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): supports Y1–Y2 'represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts' and 'recall and use addition and subtraction facts', where subtraction facts are derived from known addition bonds; underpins missing-number problems like 7 = □ − 9.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.4 'Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem. For example, subtract 10 − 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.'
• Operational details: reframe the take-away picture as a missing-part picture on a part-whole model — whole known, one part known, find the other part. Encourage counting on from the subtrahend to the minuend, especially when the parts are close (12 − 9 by counting up 9→10→11→12). This is the efficiency insight, not just an alternative.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — given 9 + □ = 13, matches it to 13 − 9 and finds 4. Tier B (age 7) — chooses to count on for 12 − 9 because the numbers are close, and explains why. Tier C (age 7+) — states that every subtraction can be rewritten as an addition with a missing part and uses it to solve/check.
bestPractices: Anchor on the part-whole model: subtraction reveals a missing PART when the whole and one part are known.
Teach counting-up (shopkeeper's method) explicitly as the efficient strategy when subtrahend and minuend are close.
Pair each subtraction with its unknown-addend twin (13 − 9 = ? ↔ 9 + ? = 13) so the equivalence is repeatedly seen.
Use missing-number equations in varied positions to force the additive reading rather than a take-away action.
Delay pure take-away drilling; contrast 'how many are left' with 'how many more to reach' so difference/missing-part meanings are established.
keyRepresentations: Part-whole (cherry) diagram with the missing part as the unknown
Bar model: total bar with one part shaded and the gap to find
Empty number line showing a count-on jump from subtrahend to minuend
Double ten-frame with one frame filled and the gap to ten visible
Fact-family triangle linking the whole and its two parts
commonMisconceptions: Believing subtraction can only mean 'take away / count back', so refusing to count up.
Not seeing 8 + ? = 10 and 10 − 8 = ? as the same question.
Counting back inefficiently for close numbers (12−11 counted back eleven steps) and making errors.
Confusing which quantity is the whole and which is a part in the part-whole model.
Treating the answer to 8 + ? = 10 as 10 (writing the whole) rather than the missing part.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year-olds understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem: 12 − 9 = ? asks the same question as 9 + ? = 12 — find the missing PART of a known whole. Anchor the equivalence on a part-whole model, teach counting up from the subtrahend when the numbers are close, and repeatedly pair each subtraction with its addition twin. A linked part-whole/number-line display can make the 'same gap, two routes' insight concrete; dialogue draws out the justification; matching and missing-number tasks consolidate; a static part-whole picture (with a double ten-frame and fact-family triangle as further representations) anchors both equations against one diagram.

activities.title: Two routes, one gap: linked part-whole and number line
feedback: When both routes land on the same gap, say: 'Taking away and counting up reached the same number — because they are the same question asked two ways.'
If the child gets 4 on 12 − 9 by counting back including the start (or by counting up starting on 9), replay the count-up: 9→10→11→12 is three jumps; count them together on the line.
If the child writes the whole (12) as the missing addend, point to the gap on the bar: 'We already know this part is 9; we are looking for the piece that fills the rest up to 12.'
activities.rationale: Showing the same situation two ways at once — take-away and count-on landing on one gap — can make the unknown-addend equivalence visible from a single action, and close-number cases let the child feel why counting up is often more efficient. Dragging to remove, hopping up the line, and the two equations updating together are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.

Missing-addend problems are conceptually harder than take-away and children often solve subtraction by counting back even when counting up is more efficient; deriving subtraction from known addition facts is a documented strategy.
Y1–Y2 pupils represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts and solve missing-number problems, deriving subtraction facts from addition bonds.
learnerActions: Look at a part-whole bar with whole 10 and known part 8, and a number line beside it.
First try to count BACK from the whole by the known part (back 8 from 10) to find the missing part; notice this is fiddly for some pairs.
Then start at the known part (8) and hop UP to the whole (8→9→10), counting the jumps to find the gap.
See both routes highlight the SAME gap of 2, and read the two printed sentences 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10 together.
Repeat with a close-number case such as 12 − 9: count back nine steps, then instead start at 9 and hop up 9→10→11→12 (three easy jumps), and see 12 − 9 = 3 printed above 9 + 3 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: A subtraction and its unknown-addend twin ask the same question — the missing part of a whole — and counting up from the subtrahend is often the shortcut, especially when the numbers are close.

activities.title: Explain why counting up works
feedback: If the child says the two are 'different sums', put 12 as the whole and 9 as a known part on a part-whole model and show the single missing part answers BOTH questions.
Affirm reasoning that names the missing part: 'Yes — the number you add to 9 to reach 12 is the same as the number left when you take 9 from 12.'
activities.rationale: The equivalence is a reasoning insight, so inviting the child to explain why counting up works and to state the addition twin targets the conceptual 'understand as' objective. Responsive spoken discussion lets a tutor probe the justification directly; recognition-only tasks would not elicit this spoken justification.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
learnerActions: Solve a close-number subtraction such as 12 − 9 using whatever method you choose.
Answer aloud: 'You could take 9 away — but is there a quicker way to get from 9 up to 12?'
State the matching addition sentence (9 + ? = 12) for the subtraction.
Explain in your own words why 12 − 9 and 9 + ? = 12 are the same question.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the equivalence — not just produce the number — shows the child reads subtraction additively rather than only as take-away.

activities.title: Match, fill, and choose the quicker route
feedback: For 9 + □ = 13: the missing part is 4, not 13 — 13 is the whole; underline the gap being asked for.
For the 'quicker route' choice, affirm counting up for 12 − 9 because 9 and 12 are close (three jumps) while counting back nine steps invites errors.
If the child reverses whole and part, restate: the whole is the total; the two parts add to it.
activities.rationale: Matching, missing-number and strategy-choice tasks consolidate an already-built idea. A fixed sequence of items consolidates and checks recognition and strategy choice rather than letting the child freely toggle representations, so it is best used after the linked model and paired with an explanation prompt.

learnerActions: Match each subtraction to its unknown-addend twin, e.g. 13 − 9 ↔ 9 + □ = 13.
Fill in the missing addend: 9 + □ = 13 (answer 4), then write the matching subtraction 13 − 9 = 4.
Decide which is quicker for 12 − 9 — counting up or counting back — and give a reason.
Given a known fact such as 8 + 5 = 13, write a subtraction you can now answer straight away.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the pairing of subtraction with its addition twin and the strategic choice of counting up when numbers are close.

activities.title: One diagram, both equations (anchor)
feedback: Point at the gap: 'This is the part we are finding — it completes 8 up to 10.'
If the child names the whole as the answer, re-point to the known part and the gap.
On the ten-frame, the empty cells show the same gap (2 empty cells when 8 of 10 are filled); on the triangle, the whole sits apart from its two parts.
activities.rationale: A static part-whole picture can present both equations against one diagram and reveal the missing part, which anchors the equivalence; a double ten-frame and fact-family triangle offer the same structure in other forms. It does not let the child act out take-away and count-on as the same gap, so use it as an anchor or for learners who need a settled reference rather than as the primary builder.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
learnerActions: Look at a part-whole diagram with a tappable whole and one known part.
Tap or lift a flap to reveal the missing part.
Read both equation forms shown side by side against the same diagram, e.g. 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10.
Name which number is the whole and which are the parts.

Compare the same whole and parts in other representations — a ten-frame with 8 cells filled and the gap of 2 to ten visible (use a double ten-frame for wholes above 10, e.g. 9 filled plus 3 more to reach 12), and a fact-family triangle linking the whole and its two parts — and read how each shows the missing part.
activities.intendedInsight: Both the subtraction and its addition twin describe the same part-whole picture, and the answer is the missing part.

constraints: Target ages 6–7; this bridges take-away toward the additive structure of subtraction.

The static part-whole picture and the matching/missing-number tasks consolidate or anchor; they do not let the child freely toggle between the take-away and count-on views, which the linked model provides.

Matching and multiple-choice items check recognition and strategy choice; they do not by themselves elicit the child's own spoken or written justification of why the two questions share an answer — pair them with an explanation prompt.

Teach counting up explicitly as the efficient strategy when subtrahend and minuend are close; do not present it as universally faster — for a pair like 12 − 3, counting back three is quicker, so prompt strategy choice by how near the numbers are.
Delay pure take-away drilling; contrast 'how many are left' with 'how many more to reach' so both difference and missing-part meanings are established.

Watch the count-up step count: 9→10→11→12 is three jumps; starting the count on the subtrahend itself (or counting back including the start) produces an off-by-one error (answer 4). This is a procedural slip, not a conceptual one — model the count rather than reteaching the concept.

The source marks the DfE National Curriculum claim as verified:true and the CCSS 1.OA.4 and Cognitively Guided Instruction claims as verified:false; these flags were not re-checked here.

The recommendation narrative for 12 − 9 uses a gap of 3 (9→10→11→12), while the worked example for 10 − 8 uses a gap of 2 (8→9→10); both are arithmetically correct. Confirmed 9 + 3 = 12 and 8 + 2 = 10, and 9 + 4 = 13.

The off-by-one answer of 4 for 12 − 9 arises from miscounting the up-jumps (counting the start) or counting back including the start; handled as a strategy/counting fix, not a conceptual reteach, consistent with the source.

probeDeeper: You found 3. In this story, is 3 a part or the whole? How do you know?
What's your evidence that 9 + 3 and 12 − 9 have the same answer?

assess.correctAnswer: 3 — and explains that 12 − 9 asks the same question as 9 + ? = 12: the number you add to 9 to reach 12 is the same as the number left when you take 9 from 12, so both give 3. Often solved by counting up from 9.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Subtraction just means take away, so it isn't an adding question' — gets 3 by counting back but insists 12−9 and 9+?=12 are different, unrelated sums.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place on a part-whole model: put 12 as the whole and 9 as a known part, and show the single missing part answers BOTH questions; do not drill more take-away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: solves the subtraction yet cannot connect it to the addition, or calls them 'different sums'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The answer to 9 + ? = 12 is 12' — writes the whole (or adds the visible numbers) instead of the missing part.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the part-whole diagram to name which piece is the whole and which is the unknown part; point at the gap that is being asked for.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked the addition twin, says 12 (the total) rather than 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back for close numbers and slips by one (starts the count on 9 rather than the first step), giving 4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — model counting UP for close numbers and prompt strategy choice by how near the numbers are; check the count with fingers or a number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 4; on watching, counts '9, 10, 11, 12' as four steps or counts back including the start.

responseLevels.gap: Solves only by counting back (or not at all) and treats 12−9 and 9+?=12 as unrelated; cannot state the matching addition.
responseLevels.full: Explains that 12−9 and 9+?=12 ask the same thing (the missing part of a whole), chooses to count up when the numbers are close, and uses a known addition fact to answer a new related subtraction.
responseLevels.partial: Gets 3 and, when prompted, can state 9+3=12, but treats it as a separate fact — cannot explain why the two questions share an answer and does not transfer to a new pair.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a subtraction: 12 − 9. Work out the answer. Then tell me how this is the same as the addition 9 + ? = 12.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds only a take-away conception can still reach 3 by counting back, but stalls or denies the link on the second tier — they cannot say why 9 + ? = 12 gives the same result. A child with the unknown-addend concept answers the 'why' immediately and frequently prefers counting up because the numbers are close. The REASON tier separates the two even when both produce the numeric answer.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Missing number problems (age 7+)
topic.description: Solve addition and subtraction problems including missing-number problems, using number facts, place value, and more complex methods
evidence: Solve a missing-number problem such as 245 + ? = 380
Choose an appropriate method (mental, written, or combination) based on the numbers
Solve multi-step problems combining addition and subtraction of three-digit numbers
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums with a hidden number — like '? − 38 = 24' or '53 + ? = 91' — by thinking carefully about what the equation is asking?

pedagogy.summary: Missing-number problems (245 + ? = 380) push children beyond 'compute the answer' to reasoning about the STRUCTURE of an equation: what is unknown, and how the inverse relationship or a count-on finds it. The equals sign must be read relationally ('is the same as'), not as 'the answer comes next'. Children choose a method from the numbers — count-on to find a missing addend, inverse to undo, or a written method — and increasingly combine steps with three-digit numbers.
bestPractices: Establish the equals sign as 'is the same as / balances', using balance and bar-model images, so a missing addend isn't read as 'add the two numbers shown'
Teach missing addend as either count-on (245 up to 380) or inverse (380 − 245); missing minuend/subtrahend via the inverse
Represent with a bar model so the unknown's position (part vs whole) dictates the operation
Choose method by the numbers — near numbers invite counting up, others a written method
Check by substituting the found number back into the original equation
keyRepresentations: Bar model / part-whole (unknown part vs unknown whole)
Balance scale image (both sides equal)
Number line (count-on to find a difference)
Equation with a box for the unknown
Base-ten / columns for the calculation
commonMisconceptions: Operator view of '=': for 245 + ? = 380 computing 245 + 380 ('the answer goes after the equals')
Not using the inverse — guessing/trial instead of 380 − 245 or counting on
Position confusion: treating ? − 120 = 250 as 250 − 120
Choosing subtraction/addition by habit rather than by where the unknown sits

learn.summary: Missing-number problems (e.g. 245 + □ = 380) move children from 'compute the answer' to reasoning about an equation's structure: what is unknown, where it sits, and how an inverse operation or a count-on finds it. The equals sign is read relationally ('is the same as / balances'), not as 'the answer comes next'. Children choose a method from the numbers — count-on for a missing addend, inverse to undo, or a written method — check by substituting back, and increasingly combine steps with three-digit numbers.

activities.title: Balance the equation: find the missing number
feedback: If a child puts 380 (or 245 + 380) in the box, point to the overloaded side: 'Both sides must match — is this side the same as 380 now?' Let them see it is far too big.

For □ − 120 = 250, if the child computes 250 − 120, use a part-whole bar: the box is the WHOLE, and we know a part (120) and what is left (250), so we add: 250 + 120 = 370. Ask: must the starting number be bigger or smaller than 250?
For 500 − □ = 340, show that the box is a part being taken away: 500 − 340 = 160, or count up 340 → 500.
If a child guesses or stalls, model two routes for a missing addend — count on from 245 to 380, and subtract 380 − 245 — and connect them as a fact family (245 + 135 = 380 ⇔ 380 − 245 = 135).
Praise correct substitution checks: 'You put 135 back and both sides came to 380 — that proves it.'
activities.rationale: A manipulable balance or bar model makes the unknown's position visible and lets the child test values, so the 'answer comes next' misreading may be confronted in action rather than only asserted. A relational view of '=' is reported to need explicit teaching over time, supported by non-standard equations and pan-balance/seesaw images.
sourceClaims: Children commonly hold an operational ('do something / put the answer next') rather than relational ('is the same value as') view of '='; Falkner, Levi & Carpenter (1999) found only 5% of grade 1-2 students answered 7 to 8 + 4 = □ + 5, most answering 12 (left side only) or 17 (sum of all numbers). A relational understanding must be explicitly taught over time, aided by non-standard equations and a pan-balance/seesaw.
Year 3 pupils solve problems, including missing-number problems, using number facts, place value and more complex addition and subtraction, and use inverse operations to check.
learnerActions: Work with a balance or bar model showing 245 and an empty box on one side and 380 on the other, with the beam tilted.
Try putting 380 in the box and observe that the side becomes far too heavy (245 + 380 = 625) — much more than 380.
Adjust the box until the two sides match, finding 135, and say in words why 135 balances it.
Use a number-line route for the same problem: start at 245 and count on to 380, noticing the jump is 135.
Repeat with the unknown in other positions, e.g. □ − 120 = 250 (answer 370) and 500 − □ = 340 (answer 160), deciding each time whether the missing quantity is a part or the whole.
Check every answer by substituting it back into the original equation (does 245 + 135 really equal 380?).
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign means the two sides are the same value; the position of the unknown (part vs whole) decides whether you add or subtract, and you can verify an answer by putting it back.

activities.title: True-or-false equations and choosing a strategy
feedback: If a child marks '245 + 380 = 380' as true, revisit the balance idea: the left side comes to 625, so the two sides are not the same value.
When near numbers appear, prompt 'these are close — would counting up be quicker?'; for far-apart numbers, a written subtraction may be easier.
Reinforce that method choice should follow the unknown's position and the numbers, not habit.
activities.rationale: True/false sorting and method-selection items can target the operator view of equals and prompt flexible strategy choice. These checking-style tasks confirm and diagnose reasoning but do not themselves require the child to construct a method, so they are best paired with the constructive balance/bar work.
sourceClaims: Children commonly hold an operational ('do something / put the answer next') rather than relational ('is the same value as') view of '='; Falkner, Levi & Carpenter (1999) found only 5% of grade 1-2 students answered 7 to 8 + 4 = □ + 5, most answering 12 (left side only) or 17 (sum of all numbers). A relational understanding must be explicitly taught over time, aided by non-standard equations and a pan-balance/seesaw.
learnerActions: Sort equations as true or false — e.g. '245 + 135 = 380' (true) and '245 + 380 = 380' (false, since 245 + 380 = 625) — to challenge the 'answer-next' habit.
For each of several missing-number problems with the box in different positions, say whether you would count on or use the inverse, and explain what about the numbers made you choose.
Solve and then justify: in 245 + □ = 380 the box is a part; in □ − 120 = 250 the box is the whole.
Check each solution by substitution before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Equations assert that both sides are equal and can be judged true or false; the choice between counting on and using the inverse depends on where the unknown sits and on how near the numbers are.

activities.title: Static balance/bar model as a reference
feedback: Prompt the child to name which quantity is missing and whether it is a part or the whole before deciding to add or subtract.
If the two revealed totals differ, ask what would make them match.
activities.rationale: A fixed diagram cannot be adjusted to test candidate values, but it serves as a useful reference for the part/whole structure and for what 'balances' means. Use it alongside, not instead of, tasks where the child tests values.
learnerActions: Study a labelled balance or part-whole bar diagram that shows which quantity is a part and which is the whole.
Tap or point to each side to reveal its total and whether the two sides match.
Use the diagram as a reference while solving problems, naming part and whole before choosing an operation.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear diagram of what balances and of part-vs-whole gives a stable mental image to reason from when identifying the unknown.

constraints: Establish '=' as 'is the same as / balances' before missing-addend work, so the box is not read as 'add the two numbers shown'.
Vary the unknown's position across all addend, minuend, subtrahend, result and whole placements; a diet of result-position problems lets position confusion go undetected.
Always require a substitution check against the original equation.

True/false and multiple-choice items primarily confirm and diagnose reasoning; they do not by themselves require the child to construct a strategy, so pair them with tasks where the child finds and justifies the missing number.
A static diagram is a reference only: it cannot let the child test candidate values, so it supports but does not replace manipulable or written solving.
Connect count-on and inverse as fact families so children can move between them rather than relying on one by habit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were not re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row judged a conversation 'poor' because 'talk cannot supply the balancing/positioning practice' and that a third dimension 'adds nothing'. These are catalog-format judgements, not established pedagogical laws; spoken explanation and justification can support this learning, so they were softened/omitted rather than asserted as universal limits.
Efficacy of the live-balance format over other media is not established by the sources; activity 1's rationale now uses 'may be confronted' rather than claiming the misreading is defeated.

Worked values verified against the original: 245 + 135 = 380; 380 − 245 = 135; for □ − 120 = 250 the whole is 250 + 120 = 370; for 500 − □ = 340 the part is 500 − 340 = 160; and 245 + 380 = 625 (the deliberate 'too big' demonstration). All consistent with the source's stated answers 135, 370, 160.

probeDeeper: Point to what's unknown in 245 + □ = 380 — is it a part or the whole? So do you add or subtract?
Substitute your answer back in — does 245 + 135 really equal 380?
For □ − 120 = 250, should the missing number be bigger or smaller than 250? Why?
Which of these did you count on for, and which did you subtract — what about the numbers made you choose?

errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a balance/bar model to re-establish '=' as 'the same as'; both sides must match. Sort true/false equations to break the 'answer next' habit.

responseLevels.gap: Adds the two visible numbers (operator view), or subtracts regardless of the box's position; no inverse/count-on strategy.
responseLevels.full: Reads '=' relationally, reasons from the unknown's position (part vs whole) to choose count-on or inverse, solves the box in any position, and checks by substituting back.
responseLevels.partial: Solves missing-addend problems (box in the result position) but is thrown when the unknown is the minuend/whole, or finds answers without checking by substitution.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three missing-number problems and watch how the child finds each, letting them choose a method: 245 + □ = 380, then □ − 120 = 250, then 500 − □ = 340. Notice whether they use the inverse or count on, and whether the position of the box changes what they do.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 245+□=380 exposes the operator view of '=' (a child adds 245+380). □−120=250 exposes position confusion (a child does 250−120 instead of 250+120). 500−□=340 checks flexible inverse/count-on. A child who reads '=' relationally and reasons from the unknown's position gets all three; a left-to-right computer fails predictably.

topic.name: Two-Step Equations
topic.description: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations; represent problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity
evidence: Solve a two-step problem that combines addition/subtraction with multiplication/division
Write an equation using a letter for the unknown (e.g. 3 × n + 5 = 26)
Assess the reasonableness of the answer using estimation and mental computation
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write an equation like 'n + 25 = 60' to represent a word problem, and then solve it to find what n equals?

pedagogy.summary: The bridge from word problem to algebraic NOTATION: solve two-step problems mixing addition/subtraction with multiplication/division, and represent the problem as an equation with a letter for the unknown (e.g. 3 × n + 5 = 26). Two conceptual hurdles sit here beyond the arithmetic — the letter must be understood as a NUMBER we do not yet know (not a label for an object), and '=' must be read RELATIONALLY ('is the same value as', so the equation can be undone by keeping both sides balanced) rather than as 'work out the answer'. Solve by inverse operations in the correct order, and check reasonableness by substitution/estimation.

learn.summary: Learners bridge from a two-step word problem to algebraic notation: solve problems that mix addition/subtraction with multiplication/division, write the problem as an equation using a letter for the unknown (e.g. 3 × n + 5 = 26), solve by inverse operations in the correct order, and check by substitution/estimation. activities.title: Balance-scale equation bench
feedback: If a learner says 'n is pencils' or 'n is packs', respond: 'n is HOW MANY pencils are in one pack — a number we have not found yet.' Point to the numeric slot and contrast with the revealed 7.
If a learner takes 5 off only one pan, show that the scale tips: whatever you do to one side you must do to the other to keep it balanced.
If a learner tries to divide by 3 before removing the 5, show on the pans that the 5 loose cubes sit OUTSIDE the 3 equal boxes, so they must come off first.
When the box opens to 7, prompt: 'put 7 back into the equation — does it come to 26?'
activities.rationale: A balance makes the letter a concrete hidden-number box and makes 'keep both sides equal' a felt constraint, engaging the letter-as-object and operator-view-of-equals misconceptions. Interactive controls such as dragging boxes/cubes onto pans, removing items from both pans, and opening a box to reveal its value make the balancing mechanism visible; these are illustrative affordances, not required technology, and their comparative efficacy is not established by the cited sources.

learnerActions: Model the story 'Maya has 3 packs of pencils plus 5 loose pencils, 26 pencils in total' by placing 3 identical unknown boxes (each labelled n) and 5 single cubes on the left pan, against 26 cubes on the right pan.
To find what is inside one box, keep the scale level: remove 5 cubes from BOTH pans, leaving the 3 boxes on the left against 21 cubes on the right.
Share the remaining 21 equally among the 3 boxes, and open a box to reveal 7 inside each.
Write the matching equation 3 × n + 5 = 26 next to the balance, and state in words what n stands for.
Substitute n = 7 back: check that 3 × 7 + 5 = 26.
activities.intendedInsight: The letter box held a NUMBER (7) all along, and it could only be found by doing the SAME thing to both sides, so '=' means genuinely balanced. The +5 is undone before the ×3 because the +5 is the last operation built — undo the last operation first — and removing it from both pans keeps them level.

activities.title: From bar model to equation, then undo in reverse
feedback: If a learner writes a running chain like 3 × n = ... + 5 = 26, show that this reads left-to-right; rewrite it as one balanced equation with both sides equal.
If a learner does 26 ÷ 3 first, point to the bar: the 5 sits outside the 3 equal groups, so subtract it before sharing.

If a learner uses the letter as a label for the object (e.g. 'n means pencils' or 'n is the pack'), restate that n is a number — the count inside one pack. Saying 'n pencils in each pack' is correct, because there n is the number of pencils.
If the check does not give 26 (e.g. n = 10 gives 35), that is the signal the order or arithmetic needs revisiting.
activities.rationale: Mapping the bar model to the symbolic equation gives the structure before notation and makes the order of inverse operations visible, supporting correct order-of-operations and the order of undoing expected by the curriculum.

learnerActions: Draw a bar model for the story: three equal boxes (each n) joined to a small part of 5, with the whole bar equal to 26.
Use the bar structure to write the equation 3 × n + 5 = 26, naming the unknown box with the letter.
List the undo steps in order on an empty number line or in writing: 26 − 5 = 21, then 21 ÷ 3 = 7.
Say aloud why the −5 comes before the ÷3 (the +5 was the last thing built, so it is undone first).

activities.intendedInsight: The structure of the problem (equal groups plus an extra part) determines the equation and the ORDER of undoing. Solving reverses the build: the last operation done is undone first.

activities.title: Match the story to the right equation, then solve in order
feedback: If a learner picks 3 + n × 5 = 26, compare it against the story: there are 3 equal packs (×) plus 5 loose (+), so the structure is 3 × n + 5.
If the steps are ordered division-before-subtraction, remind them to undo the last-built operation first.
Always require the substitution step: the value is only accepted once it makes both sides equal.
activities.rationale: Selecting and ordering supports translation and procedural accuracy. This recognition/ordering format checks whether a learner can identify the correct structure, but it does not by itself require them to construct an equation unprompted — pair it with the production tasks above.

learnerActions: Read a short scenario and choose the equation that correctly represents it, rejecting distractors such as 3 + n × 5 = 26 that misplace the operations.
Order the solving steps correctly (subtract first, then divide), filling in each result.
Substitute the found value back into the chosen equation to confirm it holds.
Explain in one sentence what the letter stands for.
activities.intendedInsight: Translating a story into the correct equation forces attention to operation order, and verifying by substitution confirms the solution rather than trusting the arithmetic blindly.

activities.title: Annotated worked example as reference
feedback: Prompt learners to name what n means before reading the solution, so the letter is tied to a number rather than an object.
After reading, have them cover the worked steps and reconstruct the solution to confirm understanding.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated example cannot be manipulated like a balance, but it is a useful reference for connecting each symbol to the story and modelling the solving order; follow it with learner-constructed solving.
learnerActions: Study a worked example that lays out the scenario, the equation 3n + 5 = 26, and the undo-steps.
For each part of 3n + 5 = 26, state what it represents in the story (the 3 packs, the n per pack, the 5 loose, the 26 total).
Re-solve a fresh variant yourself after reading the example.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference links each symbol to its meaning in the story and shows the order of inverse steps, which learners can then reproduce on new problems.

activities.title: 'What does your letter mean?' challenge dialogue
feedback: If the learner cannot explain the order, send them back to the bar or balance where the 5 sits outside the 3 equal groups.
Accept 'n is a number — the count per pack' and press for the reason the order of undoing matters.
For the minus variant, check the learner undoes the −5 by adding 5 (giving 30) before dividing by 3 (giving 10), and that 3 × 10 − 5 = 25.
activities.rationale: Discussion can surface the letter-as-object and operator-equals views and prompt self-correction, though articulating a correct answer does not by itself guarantee it transfers to independent solving. The balancing action is best paired with the hands-on model, so use this dialogue to accompany, not replace, manipulation.

learnerActions: Respond to a challenge such as 'so n is pencils?' by correcting: 'no, n is a number — how many pencils are in one pack.'
Explain why you subtracted the 5 before dividing by 3 in 3 × n + 5 = 26.
Predict what changes for a variant like 3 × n − 5 = 25 and justify your undo order (here you add 5 back first, then divide by 3).

constraints: The letter must be treated as a NUMBER we do not yet know (how many in a pack), never as the object or a label for it.
'=' must be read relationally ('is the same value as'); the equation is a balance, not an instruction to 'work out the answer'.
Solve by inverse operations in the correct order: undo the last operation built first (subtract the 5 before dividing by 3).
Always include a substitution and/or estimation check: an answer is accepted only when it makes both sides equal (e.g. n = 10 gives 35, not 26, so it fails).

Recognition/ordering tasks check identification of the correct structure but do not elicit independent construction of an equation; pair them with tasks where the learner writes and solves their own equation.

Transfer to variants with subtraction (3 × n − 5 = 25, where you add 5 back before dividing) or division to confirm the method generalises.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims about letter-as-object (Kuchemann) and the operator view of '=' are drawn from secondary-age and grade 1–2 populations respectively; they motivate the misconceptions but were not themselves gathered on this exact Year 4 task.

The claim that a particular medium 'directly attacks' or is uniquely able to fix a misconception has been softened to a scoped affordance; comparative efficacy or necessity of the balance model over other representations is not established by the cited sources.

The source also considered a 3D/spatial representation and judged it poorly suited because this content is symbolic/relational, not spatial, so a spatial 3D model adds little here. This objective limitation is retained; the original's categorical 'adds nothing' phrasing is not.

topic.name: Equations with Two Unknowns
topic.description: Find pairs of numbers that satisfy an equation with two unknowns (e.g. find pairs (a, b) where a + b = 10 or 2a + b = 15)
evidence: List all whole-number pairs (a, b) where a + b = 12 with a, b > 0
Find three pairs that satisfy 2x + y = 20
Explain systematically how to generate all integer solutions to a two-variable equation within a given range
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} find different pairs of numbers that both satisfy a rule — for example, all the pairs of whole numbers that add up to 10?

pedagogy.summary: An equation with two unknowns (a + b = 12, or 2x + y = 20) does NOT have a single answer — it has many solution pairs. The child generates such pairs and, within the stated constraints (whole numbers, positive, a range), lists them SYSTEMATICALLY so none is missed and none repeated. Fixing one unknown and stepping it through its possible values in order, computing the partner each time, makes the search exhaustive and reveals the pattern. It is a Year 6 precursor to simultaneous equations, where a SECOND equation pins the pair down to one.
bestPractices: Establish first that there are MANY pairs, not one — contrast a + b = 12 with a one-variable equation like a + 7 = 12
Fix one unknown and step it through its permitted values in order (a = 1 → b = 11, a = 2 → b = 10, …), computing the partner each time so the list is complete and ordered
Record pairs in a two-column table so completeness is visible and answer 'how do you know you've found them all?'
Attend to the stated constraints (positive, whole, within a range) — they bound how many pairs exist
For 2x + y = 20, substitute the chosen x and compute y = 20 − 2x, respecting the coefficient
Link to 'what two numbers can add up to' puzzles and to plotting the pairs as points on a line

Bar / part-whole model for a + b = 12

learn.summary: Year 6 learners discover that an equation with two unknowns (e.g. a + b = 12, or 2x + y = 20) has MANY solution pairs, not one. They generate these pairs systematically by fixing one unknown and stepping it through its permitted values in order, computing the partner each time, so no pair is missed or repeated. Stated constraints (such as whole numbers, positive, or within a range) decide which pairs are valid; when values must be whole numbers within limits, the number of pairs is finite and can be counted. This is a precursor to simultaneous equations, where a second equation can usually pin the pair down to one answer.

activities.title: Build the pair-finder: sweep one unknown and watch the pairs appear
feedback: If the learner gives one pair as 'the answer' and stops: ask 'Is there another pair that works? And another?' Then fix a and step it through its values to reveal them all.
If the search is random with gaps or repeats: have them step one unknown through its values in order and record in a table — 'I know I have them all because I worked systematically.'
If they cannot say whether the list is complete: point to the ordered column of a-values and ask which values of a have not yet been tried.

Full solution for a + b = 12 (whole, > 0): (1,11), (2,10), (3,9), (4,8), (5,7), (6,6), (7,5), (8,4), (9,3), (10,2), (11,1) — 11 pairs, complete because every value of a from 1 to 11 has been tried in order.
activities.rationale: The Year 6 objective is to find pairs satisfying a two-unknown equation, framed as generating MULTIPLE pairs. Working randomly first hides which cases are missing; ordering and systematising exposes gaps and answers 'how do you know you've found them all?'. Fixing one unknown and stepping it makes the search exhaustive and reveals the linear pattern.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should 'find pairs of numbers that satisfy an equation with 2 unknowns'; the non-statutory guidance includes number puzzles such as 'what 2 numbers can add up to', framing the task as generating multiple pairs.

When children are asked to find all possibilities they first work randomly and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting and ordering their attempts exposes the gaps, and having a system is what ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
learnerActions: Before starting, compare a + b = 12 with a + 7 = 12: how many answers does each have? Notice that the one-variable equation has a single answer but the two-unknown equation has many.
Start with a + b = 12 (whole numbers, greater than 0). Set a = 1 and work out b; record (1, 11). Set a = 2 and work out b; record (2, 10). Continue in order: a = 3 → b = 9, a = 4 → b = 8, and so on.
Record each pair in an ordered two-column table (a | b) so completeness is visible.
After listing, answer: 'How many pairs are there? How do you know you have found them ALL?' State the justification: 'I tried every value of a from 1 to 11 in order.'

Optional interactive version: drag a slider for a that moves in whole-number steps from 1 to 11 and watch b recompute live so a + b = 12 always holds; each pair drops into the ordered table AND lights a point on a grid. Sweeping the slider fills the table in order while the separate points line up along a straight line — showing at once that there are many solutions and that stepping a through every permitted value catches them all.
activities.intendedInsight: An equation with two unknowns has a whole family of solution pairs; stepping one unknown through its permitted values in order generates every pair and lets you prove the list is complete.

activities.title: Let the constraints bound the count
feedback: If pairs like (0, 12), (13, −1), or decimals appear despite a 'whole, greater than 0' condition: reread the constraint together; it fixes which values of a are permitted and therefore how many pairs there are.
If allowing 0 or any whole number changes the count, ask the learner to re-list in order under the new rule and recount.
activities.rationale: Ignoring constraints produces invalid pairs and an incorrect count. Attending to the stated conditions makes the search both correct and finite, and shows why the number of pairs is what it is.
learnerActions: Reread the stated condition (whole numbers, positive, within a range) and decide which values of a are allowed before listing.
For a + b = 12 with 'whole, greater than 0', check: is (0, 12) allowed? Is (13, −1) allowed? Are decimals allowed? Explain why each is excluded by the condition.
Try a different constraint, e.g. 'a and b are whole numbers from 0 to 10 inclusive', and work out how the list of valid pairs changes and how many remain (a can now only be 2 to 10, so 9 pairs).

Optional interactive version: a constraints toggle ('whole numbers only', 'positive only', 'between 0 and 10') greys out the pairs that break the rule, so the learner SEES how the constraint bounds how many pairs exist.
activities.intendedInsight: The constraints bound which values of the stepped unknown are allowed, and therefore exactly how many valid pairs exist.

activities.title: Respect the coefficient: 2x + y = 20
feedback: If the learner offers (3, 17) for 2x + y = 20: have them substitute the numbers — 2×3 + 17 = 23 ≠ 20. The pair satisfies x + y = 20, not 2x + y = 20.
Prompt: substitute the chosen x and compute y = 20 − 2x explicitly rather than guessing a partner that sums to 20.
activities.rationale: Mishandling the coefficient (treating 2x + y as x + y) is a common error. Substituting and computing y = 20 − 2x each time makes the coefficient's role concrete and transfers the systematic method to a new two-unknown equation.
learnerActions: For 2x + y = 20, choose a value for x, then compute y = 20 − 2x explicitly — the 2 doubles x BEFORE y is added.
Find three valid pairs, e.g. x = 1 → y = 18 giving (1,18); x = 2 → y = 16 giving (2,16); x = 3 → y = 14 giving (3,14).
Check a tempting wrong pair: does (3, 17) satisfy 2x + y = 20? Substitute: 2×3 + 17 = 23, not 20. Note that (3, 17) fits x + y = 20, a different equation.
Explain in your own words how 2x + y = 20 differs from x + y = 20.
Optional interactive version: a 2x + y = 20 preset shows y recomputing as 20 − 2x as x changes, making the coefficient's effect visible.
activities.intendedInsight: A coefficient changes the partner computation: for 2x + y = 20 the partner is y = 20 − 2x, which is not the same as x + y = 20.

constraints: Establish FIRST that there are many pairs, not one — contrast a + b = 12 with a one-variable equation like a + 7 = 12.
The ordered two-column table (or a 'fix one unknown and step it' list) is essential for judging completeness; recording pairs out of order defeats the purpose.

Recognition-only or fill-in-the-blank items (complete-the-pair, categorise valid vs invalid, 'how many pairs?') can check the skill but do NOT by themselves build the systematic, exhaustive search; the learner must generate and order the pairs independently.

A static completed table beside the line of points can display the full solution set, but it does the discovery for the learner — they do not generate the pairs or test completeness themselves. Treat it as a reveal/illustration, not as the generating activity.
Plotting the pairs as points on a straight line is a bridge to graphs and simultaneous equations; keep it linked to the ordered table so the pattern connects back to the stepping method.

Interactive slider/toggle/point-lighting features named above are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; the underlying learning (stepping one unknown in order, computing the partner, justifying completeness) can also be done with pencil, paper, and a hand-drawn table.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: a + b = 12 (whole, >0) yields exactly 11 pairs (a from 1 to 11) — verified. For 2x + y = 20, y = 20 − 2x: (1,18), (2,16), (3,14) all satisfy 2x + y = 20 — verified. (3,17) gives 2×3+17 = 23 ≠ 20 and satisfies x + y = 20 instead — the distractor is correctly characterised.

The legacy row's claim that 3D and in-role dialogue formats 'add nothing' / 'cannot build' the skill was not established by the cited sources and has been removed rather than asserted as a universal law; the point retained is the narrowly scoped one that recognition-only responses do not elicit independent systematic generation.

The source claims cited in Activity 1 support the general teaching principle (generate multiple pairs; work systematically to prove completeness). No cited source directly supports the constraint-bounding principle (Activity 2) or the coefficient-handling principle (Activity 3), so those carry empty sourceClaims and remain qualified proposals.
The bar/part-whole model from the original keyRepresentations is not instantiated in these activities; it is left as an optional representation, apt for a + b = 12 but less natural for 2x + y = 20.

pedagogy.summary: Solving a linear equation means finding the value of the unknown that makes the two sides genuinely equal, by doing the SAME operation to both sides until the unknown is isolated. The relational meaning of the equals sign is the foundation: each written line must be a true equality, not a running commentary strung together with '='. The persistent errors — treating subtraction as commutative, refusing negative solutions, mishandling the unknown on both sides, and operating on one side only — are addressed with a balance model, inverse operations, and a substitution check.
bestPractices: Teach 'do the same to both sides' with a balance model so operations that keep the scale level are felt as legal and one-sided moves as illegal.
Insist on ONE valid equality per line — forbid run-on chains like 5−x=6=x=−1; each line must itself be true.
Isolate the unknown with inverse operations; for the unknown on both sides, gather it on one side by subtracting the smaller term from both.
Always check by substituting the solution back into the ORIGINAL equation.
Handle negatives explicitly (number line / zero-pairs) rather than assuming the answer must be positive; discuss whether an equation has one, none, or infinitely many solutions.
keyRepresentations: Balance scale (unknown-boxes and unit-weights; same action on both pans)
Algebra tiles with zero-pairs for negatives and unknown-on-both-sides
Inverse-operation / function-machine unwinding
Number line for negative solutions
Substitution-back check
commonMisconceptions: Treats subtraction as commutative: 5−x=6 solved as x−5=6 giving x=11.
Considers positive numbers only, so rejects or never reaches a negative solution.
Run-on / operational equals sign: writes 5−x=6=x=−1 or 3x−5=2x=x=5, using '=' to mean 'and then'.
Mishandles the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x): stops at 'unlike terms' or subtracts incorrectly.
Performs an operation on one side only, unbalancing the equation.
Thinks every equation has exactly one solution (misses none/infinitely-many).

learn.summary: Solving a linear equation means finding the value of the unknown that makes both sides genuinely equal, by doing the SAME operation to both sides until the unknown is isolated. The relational meaning of '=' is the foundation: each written line must itself be a true equality, not a running commentary strung together with '='. Target the persistent errors — treating subtraction as commutative, refusing negative solutions, mishandling the unknown on both sides, and operating on one side only — with a balance model, inverse operations, explicit handling of negatives, and a substitution check back into the original equation.

activities.title: Balance-scale solver: keep both pans level
feedback: If a one-sided action is attempted: the scale tips because the two sides are no longer equal; redo the same action on both pans.

When isolating 8x − 6 = 2x: after removing 2 x-boxes from each side you have 6x − 6 = 0; adding 6 to both sides gives 6x = 6; dividing both sides by 6 gives x = 1. Substitute back: 8(1) − 6 = 2 and 2(1) = 2 — equal, so x = 1 checks.
For 5 − x = 6: using zero-pairs gives −x = 1, so x = −1. Substitute back: 5 − (−1) = 6 — correct; note 5 − x is NOT the same as x − 5.
activities.rationale: 'Do the same to both sides' is a physical intuition made legal-feeling by a balance the learner must keep level; illegal one-sided moves visibly tip it, so the rule is enforced by the model. Dragging actions onto both pans, live tipping, and zero-pair anti-weights are offered as concrete ways to make the balancing mechanism visible; they are examples, not the only possible setup, and are proposed rather than validated as superior to other media.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
Children frequently read the equals sign operationally ('work out the answer') rather than relationally (the two sides are equal), which underlies run-on chains and difficulty balancing equations.
learnerActions: Represent an equation as two pans: unknown-boxes (x) and unit-weights, using 'anti-weights' (zero-pairs) for any negative amount. Set up 8x − 6 = 2x with the −6 shown as six anti-weights on that pan.

Choose an action (add or remove the same number of units, using zero-pairs where a pan has none to remove; remove an x-box; halve everything) and apply it to BOTH pans at once; watch the scale stay level.
Try a one-sided action on purpose and observe that the scale tips — that move is not allowed because it breaks the equality.

Solve 8x − 6 = 2x: remove 2 x-boxes from each pan to reach 6x − 6 = 0, then add 6 units to each pan (cancelling the six anti-weights) to reach 6x = 6, then divide both pans into 6 equal groups (÷6) to reach x = 1.

Use an anti-x-box for −x, plus unit zero-pairs, to model 5 − x = 6: remove 5 units from both pans to reach −x = 1, then swap every item on both pans for its opposite (multiply both sides by −1) to reach x = −1, so the negative solution is something you build and see rather than distrust.
Write down each balanced state as its own line — one true equality per line.
activities.intendedInsight: The only way to keep the scale level while stripping it down to a single x is to mirror every move on both sides — that mirroring IS the solving method, and a negative result is a legitimate, visible outcome.

activities.title: One true equality per line: fix the run-on equals sign
feedback: In 5 − x = 6 = x = −1, the middle '6 = x' is false (6 does not equal −1); the valid working is 5 − x = 6 → −x = 1 → x = −1, one true equality per line.

For 3x − 5 = 2x: subtract 2x from both sides to get x − 5 = 0, then add 5 to both sides to get x = 5. Check: 3(5) − 5 = 10 and 2(5) = 10 — equal, so x = 5. (Note the first item here, 5 − x = 6, has solution x = −1; the two tasks are different equations.)
activities.rationale: The operational (left-to-right 'compute') reading of '=' underlies run-on chains; reading written maths aloud and reformatting into vertical true equalities confronts that reading directly.
sourceClaims: Children frequently read the equals sign operationally ('work out the answer') rather than relationally (the two sides are equal), which underlies run-on chains and difficulty balancing equations.

learnerActions: Read aloud, left to right, the chain 5 − x = 6 = x = −1. Decide whether each '=' states a genuine equality (does 6 really equal x?).
Rewrite the working as a vertical chain where every single line is itself true: 5 − x = 6, then −x = 1, then x = −1.
Do the same for 3x − 5 = 2x: rewrite the run-on 3x − 5 = 2x = x = 5 as separate true lines, subtracting 2x from both sides first (3x − 5 = 2x → x − 5 = 0 → x = 5), and check by substitution.
Spot the invalid line: given a worked solution containing a run-on chain, identify which '=' is false and correct it.
activities.intendedInsight: '=' means the two sides have equal value, not 'and then'. Every line of correct working must be a standalone true statement.

activities.title: Solve, then check by substitution; classify how many solutions
feedback: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 expands to 2x + 6 = 2x + 6, true for every x, so infinitely many solutions — an identity, not a single answer.
If substitution does not make both sides equal, the solution is wrong; retrace which line first stopped being a true equality.
activities.rationale: Substitution into the original equation makes correctness self-verifiable and pushes past guess-and-check; the identity 2(x+3)=2x+6 is a concrete counterexample to 'every equation has one solution'.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
KS3 pupils should use algebraic methods to solve linear equations in one variable, including all forms that require rearrangement.
learnerActions: Solve a set of equations by inverse operations, writing one true equality per line: start with 5 − x = 6 and 8x − 6 = 2x, then extend to equations with brackets and fractional/negative coefficients.
For each solution, substitute it back into the ORIGINAL equation and confirm both sides are equal.
Solve 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 and decide what happens: after expanding the bracket, both sides are identical (2x + 6 = 2x + 6), so every value of x works — infinitely many solutions.
Construct or examine an equation that simplifies to a false statement (e.g. a contradiction) and recognise it has no solution.
Sort equations into 'one solution', 'no solution', 'infinitely many solutions'.
activities.intendedInsight: A solved equation must survive a substitution check in the original; and not every equation has exactly one solution — some have none and some have infinitely many.

activities.title: Sequenced steps and worked-solution annotation (supporting practice)
feedback: 3x + 5 = 20: subtract 5 from both sides (3x = 15), then divide both sides by 3 (x = 5); check 3(5) + 5 = 20. ✓
If a line in the annotated solution alters only one side, it is invalid — the equality no longer holds; the matching move must act on both sides.
A static worked solution can display one correct balanced chain, but it does not itself let the learner perform the balancing; pair it with the balance-scale activity where the construction happens.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and fill-in-the-line tasks make the stepwise structure explicit and can surface run-on-equals and one-sided errors through forced choices; annotation of a fixed solution can display a model chain and support recognition/consolidation, but recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own production of the balancing moves.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
learnerActions: Order the correct solving steps for 3x + 5 = 20 from a scrambled set, stating what is done to both sides at each step.
Fill in each missing line of the working for 8x − 6 = 2x, keeping one true equality per line.
For a step in progress, state what operation should be applied to both sides next.
Examine an annotated worked solution and, line by line, name the inverse operation applied to both sides; then flag any invalid line (e.g. a run-on chain like 5 − x = 6 = x = −1).
activities.intendedInsight: Solving is a reproducible sequence of 'same operation to both sides' moves, and being able to name each inverse operation and reject invalid lines consolidates the procedure.

constraints: Each written line must be a single true equality; forbid run-on chains like 5 − x = 6 = x = −1 or 3x − 5 = 2x = x = 5 where the '=' means 'and then'.
Every operation must be applied to BOTH sides; operating on one side only unbalances the equation and makes the line false.
Handle negatives explicitly (number line or zero-pairs) rather than assuming the answer must be positive; 5 − x is not the same as x − 5.
On a balance model, represent any negative amount (e.g. the −6 in 8x − 6) with anti-weights (zero-pairs) so the pans and the written equality stay consistent.
For the unknown on both sides, gather it on one side by subtracting the same term from both sides (e.g. subtract 2x from 8x − 6 = 2x to reach 6x − 6 = 0).
Always check by substituting the solution back into the ORIGINAL equation.
Discuss that an equation may have one solution, no solution, or infinitely many (e.g. the identity 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6).

A fixed/annotated worked solution and ordering/fill-in tasks support recognition and consolidation but do not elicit the learner's own balancing; they complement, rather than replace, hands-on solving where the learner performs each move.
Prerequisite support for negative-number reasoning and collecting like terms may be needed before equations with negative/fractional coefficients or the unknown on both sides.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the balance-scale approach as uniquely able to 'force' discovery and claims 3D 'adds nothing' and that a static image 'cannot' fix the misconceptions. These are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to a scoped proposal (balance model as a vivid way to make the rule visible) and the static worked solution retained as a consolidation/recognition support rather than dismissed.
The Kieran (1981) source is marked verified:false in the row; treat its support for the relational-equals principle as unconfirmed here.

Independent self-audit of worked examples: 5 − x = 6 → x = −1 (check 5 − (−1) = 6); 8x − 6 = 2x → x = 1 (check 8 − 6 = 2 = 2); 3x − 5 = 2x → x = 5 (check 10 = 10); 3x + 5 = 20 → x = 5 (check 20 = 20); 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 is an identity. The incorrect misconception outputs (x = 11 for 5 − x = 6; the run-on chains) are presented only as errors to confront, never as valid answers.

Balance-scale walkthrough is coherent: after removing 2 x-boxes the state is 6x − 6 = 0, the −6 is modelled with anti-weights so adding 6 units to both pans cancels them to 6x = 6, then ÷6 gives x = 1. Activity 0 feedback was made explicit about the ÷6 step to match the learnerActions and the 'show every line' emphasis.

The diagnostic items 5 − x = 6 and 8x − 6 = 2x are reused across activities as teaching items; they are kept as distinct equations with distinct solutions (−1 and 1) to avoid confusion when both appear in one task.

probeDeeper: Check your answer to (a) by putting it back into 5 − x = 6 — does it work?
In (b), how do you know x = 1 is the ONLY solution and not just A solution? (pushes past guess-and-check)
You wrote 5−x=6=x=−1 — read that out loud left to right. Is 6 really equal to x? (confronts the run-on equals sign)
Here is 2(x+3) = 2x + 6 — solve it. What happens, and what does that tell you about how many solutions it has? (counterexample: an identity / infinitely many solutions)

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child this card and say 'solve these, showing every line of your working': (a) 5 − x = 6 and (b) 8x − 6 = 2x. Say nothing about method. pedagogy.summary: Writing algebraic equations means translating a situation — a 'think of a number' process or a comparison — into symbols, with letters standing for the NUMBER of things (not the things themselves) and an equals sign expressing genuine equality. The two documented traps are the reversal error (mapping words left-to-right onto symbols, so '4 times as many cats as dogs' becomes 4c=d instead of c=4d) and treating letters as object-labels. Both are defeated by anchoring translation to quantities and always testing the finished equation with real numbers.
bestPractices: Model the quantity, not the word order: before writing, ask 'if there were 3 dogs, how many cats?' and build the equation to fit the numbers.
Insist letters stand for the NUMBER of things ('c = the number of cats'), never the object ('c = cats') — the label reading drives reversal.
Build process ('think of a number...') equations step-by-step with a function machine, so operations and their order are captured faithfully.
Always check the finished equation by substituting a value — 4c=d with d=3 predicts three-quarters of a dog, exposing the reversal.
Read the equation back in words and compare it to the original statement (Clement's self-check).
keyRepresentations: Bar model (a cats-bar made of 4 copies of the dogs-bar)
Function machine for 'think of a number' processes
Table of values to test a candidate equation

commonMisconceptions: Reversal error via word-order matching: '4 times as many cats as dogs' → 4c=d, mapping words directly to symbols instead of modelling the relationship.
Letter-as-object/label (static comparison): treats c as 'cats' and reads 4c=d as 'four cats for each dog', with '=' meaning correspondence not equality.
Writes an expression with no equals sign when an equation is required.
Mis-orders operations in a process translation ('double it and add 5' written wrongly), ignoring order of operations.

activities.title: Bar-model translator with a numerical reality check
feedback: If the learner writes 4c = d: substitute d = 3. The equation then claims c = 0.75 — three-quarters of a cat, and fewer cats than dogs, though the picture shows 12 cats. Ask 'can there be three-quarters of a cat? Should there be more cats or more dogs? What does that tell you about the equation?'
If c = 4d survives the substitution (d = 2 gives c = 8, matching the picture), confirm: the equation agrees with real counts.
Read the finished equation aloud in words and compare it to the original story: does 'the number of cats is four lots of the number of dogs' match?

For the process mode, if operations are misread or mis-ordered (e.g. n² + 5, which squares instead of doubling, or 2(n + 5), which adds before doubling), rebuild one step at a time and name each operation in turn.
activities.rationale: The reversal error is defeated when a wrong equation is tested against real quantities; building the situation with a bar first, then checking with numbers, makes the collision visible. An interactive slider that recolours the picture and recomputes the count as the learner sets the number of dogs is one way to make the check concrete, but the same cycle works on paper with a table of values.
sourceClaims: The reversal error is the dominant mistake in translating comparison statements to equations: Clement, Lochhead & Monk (1981) found 37% of engineering freshmen wrote 6S=P instead of S=6P, and ~68% of the incorrect responses were reversals; it stems from word-order matching (direct left-to-right mapping) or a static-comparison/letter-as-label reading, not carelessness.
learnerActions: Read a comparison statement such as '4 times as many cats as dogs'.
Before writing anything, answer 'if there were 3 dogs, how many cats?' (12) and build the picture: a cats-bar made of 4 copies of the dogs-bar.
Write the equation that fits the picture: c = 4d (equivalently 4d = c), where c = the number of cats and d = the number of dogs.
Test it: set d = 2, check that the equation gives c = 8, and confirm the picture agrees.

Deliberately try the reversed equation 4c = d, set d = 3, and see that it demands c = 0.75 — three-quarters of a cat, not the 12 cats the picture shows, and fewer cats than dogs. Notice that d = 4 gives c = 1, a whole number but still fewer cats than dogs, so compare with the picture rather than only checking for a whole number. Explain why this shows word-order matching is wrong.
In a second mode, turn a 'think of a number' process into an equation step by step, e.g. 'think of a number, double it, add 5, get 17' → 2n + 5 = 17.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading words straight into symbols left-to-right is NOT the same as modelling the relationship; testing an equation against counts built from the situation (3 dogs → 12 cats) reveals a reversed equation, which predicts fewer cats than dogs and sometimes even a non-whole count such as three-quarters of a cat.

activities.title: Function machine for process equations
feedback: If the learner writes operations in reading order regardless of the process, step through the machine box by box and rebuild the expression.
After solving, substitute the value back through the machine to confirm it produces the stated result.
activities.rationale: Building process equations step-by-step with a function machine captures operations and their order faithfully, addressing the mis-ordering misconception; connecting to order of operations supports correct notation.
learnerActions: Take a 'think of a number' process, e.g. 'think of a number, treble it, subtract 4, and you get 20'.
Feed the unknown through a function machine one operation at a time: n → ×3 → −4 → 20.
Write the equation capturing the operations in order: 3n − 4 = 20.
Find the value of n that works (n = 8), and check by substituting it back (3×8 − 4 = 20).
Contrast with a mis-ordered attempt and explain why operation order matters.
activities.intendedInsight: A process translates faithfully only when each operation and its order are captured in turn; the letter is an unknown number flowing through the machine.

activities.title: Match stories to equations, including reversal traps

sourceClaims: The reversal error is the dominant mistake in translating comparison statements to equations: Clement, Lochhead & Monk (1981) found 37% of engineering freshmen wrote 6S=P instead of S=6P, and ~68% of the incorrect responses were reversals; it stems from word-order matching (direct left-to-right mapping) or a static-comparison/letter-as-label reading, not carelessness.
learnerActions: Connect comparison statements to the correct equation, with reversal distractors present (e.g. 4c = d offered alongside c = 4d for '4 times as many cats as dogs').
Fill in the blanks of a process equation, e.g. 'think of a number, treble it, subtract 4, get 20' → __n − __ = __.
For any match you make, justify it by substituting a value — and for any distractor you rejected, say which number exposes it.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising correct translations and spotting reversal distractors sharpens the distinction between word-order matching and modelling; justification by substitution turns recognition into reasoning.

activities.title: Puzzle-setter dialogue: write, read back, and defend
feedback: If the read-back does not match the story — e.g. 4c = d read faithfully as 'four lots of the number of cats equals the number of dogs' (four dogs for every cat), whereas the story 'four times as many cats as dogs' means four cats for every dog — that mismatch signals a reversal; test it with a value.
If a letter is described as the object ('c = cats'), restate it as 'the number of cats' and substitute a value to show the letter behaves like a number.
activities.rationale: Posing situations and probing 'read it back — does it match?' rehearses the self-check and surfaces reasoning; the numerical-collision insight is made sharper when paired with an actual substitution rather than discussion alone.
learnerActions: A puzzle-setter poses a situation (process or comparison) and asks you to write an equation for it.
Read your equation back in words and judge whether it matches the original statement (Clement's read-back self-check).
When challenged ('someone wrote 4c = d for 4 times as many cats as dogs — are they right?'), argue your case using specific numbers.
State plainly what each letter stands for, e.g. 'c is the number of cats', and confirm the equals sign means equality.
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken justification and reading the equation back out loud can catch reversal and letter-as-label errors that a silent write-down may hide.

activities.title: Annotate a worked translation
feedback: After the annotation, require the learner to translate a new statement and substitute a value — the example is a model, not a substitute for constructing and testing an equation.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example does not itself run the try-and-test cycle that corrects reversal, but it can make one correct translation explicit; it is a scaffold toward independent construction, not a replacement for it.
learnerActions: Examine a finished translation such as 2n + 5 = 17.
Reveal which words of the original statement each symbol came from (n ← 'a number', ×2 ← 'double it', +5 ← 'add 5', =17 ← 'to get 17').
Then write your own equation for a fresh statement and run the number check yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the word-to-symbol mapping of a correct example clarifies what faithful translation looks like, before attempting the full try-and-test cycle independently.

constraints: Letters must stand for the NUMBER of things ('c = the number of cats'), never the object ('c = cats'); the object-label reading drives the reversal error.

Always close translation with a numerical test: substitute a value and check the equation gives the count you predicted from the situation (e.g. 3 dogs → 12 cats). A non-whole count of objects is a warning sign, but a whole answer alone does not prove the equation is right (4c = d with d = 4 gives c = 1).
An equation requires an equals sign expressing equality; an expression alone is not an equation and the equals sign does not mean correspondence.

Matching and fill-in-the-blank checks are recognition tasks: they assess and rehearse but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and defend an equation independently — pair them with construction.
A fixed annotated example is a scaffold; it does not itself run the try-and-test cycle, so follow it with learner-generated translations that are tested with numbers.
For comparison statements, build the quantities (e.g. 'if 3 dogs, then 12 cats') before writing the equation, rather than mapping words left-to-right.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The MacGregor & Stacey (1993) source is marked unverified in the row (>50% reversals among 9th graders on 'y is eight times z'); treat its figures cautiously and verify before citing.

Self-audit of the reversed-equation counterexample: for 4c = d with d = 3, the equation gives c = 3/4, i.e. three-quarters of a cat (a valid fraction but not a whole count of animals). The original text said '4c=d with d=3 predicts three-quarters of a dog' in one place and 'half a dog' in another — these conflate which animal is fractional and are inconsistent. The correct reading is that c (cats) becomes fractional; activities state three-quarters of a cat for d = 3. The 'half a dog' phrasing (from d = 2 in the recommendation) is dropped as inconsistent.

Self-audit of process arithmetic: 'double it, add 5, get 17' → 2n + 5 = 17 gives n = 6; 'treble it, subtract 4, get 20' → 3n − 4 = 20 gives n = 8; '4 times as many cats as dogs' with 3 dogs gives 12 cats — all consistent.
The claim that a 3D/spatial environment 'adds nothing' to symbolic translation was removed as a non-established universal; it is simply not developed here because the learning target is symbolic.

The DfE curriculum claim was removed from activity-level sourceClaims because it supports the objective/topic and curriculum necessity, not the specific teaching principles (numerical reality check; function-machine ordering). It remains part of the row's evidence base for the objective overall.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal error by word-order matching — writes 4c = d for '4 times as many cats as dogs', mapping the words straight onto symbols left-to-right.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor to quantities: 'if there are 3 dogs, how many cats?' (12). Does 4c = d give that? Build a small table of values BEFORE writing the equation, then read the equation aloud to check it matches.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 'four times as many cats as dogs' the child writes 4c = d, and reads it back as 'four cats for every dog'; the equation fails a numerical test.

errorPatterns.pattern: Letter-as-object / static comparison — treats c as 'cats' and the equals sign as correspondence, not the NUMBER of cats and equality.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Restate every letter as 'the number of ___'; substitute a value to show the letter behaves like a number, not a name.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Interprets 2n+5=17 as involving a thing called n rather than an unknown number; in translation uses letters as units/labels ('c cats').

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-orders operations when translating a process — 'double it and add 5' written with the operations in the wrong order or notation reversed.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the expression one step at a time with a function machine, capturing each operation in turn; connect to order of operations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes something like n2+5, or applies the operations in reading order regardless of the process described.

responseLevels.gap: Maps words directly to symbols (4c=d) or treats letters as object-labels; the equation does not survive a numerical check, and interpreting a given equation is vague or thing-based.
responseLevels.full: Translates both process and comparison statements so they survive a numerical check, interprets a given equation back into a matching story, treats letters as numbers of things, and self-corrects by substituting values or reading the equation back.
responseLevels.partial: Translates simple one-operation and process statements correctly and interprets a given equation's operations, but reverses or mis-models comparison ('times as many') statements, or is inconsistent about whether the letter is a number.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two parts. First (interpret): show the child 2n + 5 = 17 and ask 'in words, what is this saying, and what does n stand for?' Then (translate): 'Now write an equation for this — At the shelter there are 4 times as many cats as dogs. Use c for the number of cats and d for the number of dogs.' Listen and watch what they write; offer no options.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The translate direction separates the reasoners: a child who models quantities writes c = 4d and can justify it with numbers; a child using word-order matching writes 4c = d ('4 times cats as dogs', straight off the sentence) and reads it back as 'four cats per dog'. The interpret direction exposes letter-as-label — saying n is the tag 'number' rather than a particular unknown number to be found.
